entries.title: Sharing catalog metadata across data platforms, engines, and agents
entries.summary: We’re excited to announce support for catalog labels – a new capability in the Apache...
entries.content:
Make table and column context accessible for discovery, governance, and agentic workflows.

by Daniel Weeks, Andrei Tserakhau, Jason Reid, Michelle Leon and Alex Jiang

  • Catalog labels provide a standard way to share table- and column-level context through the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API.
  • Unity Catalog is implementing the standard to make its tags consumable by any tool and platform.
  • Databricks, Google Cloud, Salesforce, ClickHouse, Atlan, Collibra, DataHub, Immuta, Trust3 AI, PhoenixAI, and Datastrato are aligned with the vision of catalog metadata exchange across the data and AI ecosystem.

We’re excited to announce support for catalog labels – a new capability in the Apache Iceberg™ REST Catalog API that enables platforms, engines, and agents to access context such as business purpose, ownership and data classifications maintained in Iceberg REST-compatible catalogs. This shared context supports discovery, governance, and agentic workflows across the data and AI ecosystem.

We believe that catalog metadata should be as open and portable as the data it describes. As enterprises bring more tools into their open lakehouse architectures, they need a common way to share the context that makes their data understandable, useful, and secure for all teams, regardless of what tools they use.

Today, that context often remains siloed in the source catalog. Data and AI teams must recreate classifications across platforms, maintain custom metadata synchronization pipelines, or work with agents that lack complete context.

Databricks is joined by Google Cloud, Salesforce, ClickHouse, Atlan, Collibra, DataHub, Immuta, Trust3 AI, PhoenixAI, and Datastrato in advancing this shared vision of metadata interoperability. Catalog labels offer a path toward that vision, making catalog context portable while allowing each platform to retain its own capabilities and controls.

Databricks worked with the Apache Iceberg community to add an optional labels field to the Iceberg REST LoadTable response. This gives catalogs a standard way to expose table- and column-level context to other platforms, tools, and agents.

“We're excited to see catalog labels take shape in the Apache Iceberg community as an open protocol for exchanging live, table and column-level governance tags across catalogs and engines. This complements Open Knowledge Format (OKF) as a higher-level standard for portable business semantics and cross-system knowledge, giving enterprises a clean, layered foundation from catalog metadata to AI-ready context.”- Gaurav Saxena, Director of Product Management, Google Cloud

Labels are string key-value pairs that can describe business ownership, intended use, sensitivity or other catalog-maintained context. The standard defines a common format for sharing this metadata without prescribing its vocabulary or interpretation, giving each platform the flexibility to build on it in its own way.

Consider a table named support_cases

Field ID Column Type
1 case_id string
2 opened_at timestamp
3 issue_summary string

An authorized data steward assigns domain=customer_support and the Databricks system tag system.certification_status=certified to the table, and content_type=support_case_summary to the issue_summary column.

A catalog exposing these tags could include the following in its Iceberg REST LoadTable response:

This example shows only the labels portion of the response.

A downstream platform can then use these labels to make the table more useful:

  • Improve discovery. A catalog can surface the business domain and intended purpose in search results, helping users identify relevant data without asking stewards to recreate that context.
  • Give agents better context. An agent investigating support issues could use domain=customer_support and system.certification_status=certified to identify a relevant dataset, then use the column label to locate case summaries.
  • Connect classifications to policies. A governance platform could map a sensitivity label to a locally defined masking rule, with the receiving platform responsible for configuring and enforcing that rule.

For example, PyIceberg has added support for accessing catalog labels in Python. In the next 0.13 release, applications will be able to inspect the table- and column-level labels from the same support_cases table:

This produces:

These labels make the catalog’s metadata available directly to Python applications, including data-discovery tools and agents.

Unity Catalog exposes its table- and column-level tags through catalog labels with Tag Exchange. Tag Exchange is a step toward our broader vision of open governance: context maintained in one system should be usable across every platform, engine, and AI agent working with the data.

“Classification is only useful if it reaches the place where access is decided. Tag Exchange gets it there. For the enterprises we work with, a sensitivity label set once in Unity Catalog can now drive policy in platforms like Trust3 AI without a separate metadata project.”- Don Bosco Durai, CTO, Trust3 AI

By exposing Unity Catalog’s table- and column-level tags, Tag Exchange lets enterprises reuse classifications and business context for discovery, agent workflows, and access policies. Each tool has the freedom to decide how to interpret and use that context.

“A company’s context, like what its data means, who owns it, and how it may be used, is its IP. It should be as portable as the data it describes, and Atlan is excited to partner with Databricks on this mission. Open metadata exchange through the Iceberg REST Catalog lets enterprises keep that context intact across every platform they choose to run.”- Chandru Sugunan, Director of Product, Atlan

Databricks is excited to join our partners in advancing catalog labels to make catalog metadata open and accessible.

"With our continued commitment to open Iceberg standards, we’re excited to work with Databricks and the broader ecosystem to enable metadata sharing across the customer data estate, helping AI and agents operate with consistent business semantics.”- Narinder Singh, VP, Product Management, Salesforce

Together, we’re in support of an open interface that gives AI agents and data platforms shared context for discovering data, understanding it, and keeping it governed.

Tag Exchange is available in Beta today, exposing Unity Catalog’s table- and column-level tags through catalog labels. To get started, enable “Tag Exchange via Iceberg REST Catalog” in the Databricks Previews portal.

Catalog labels are string key-value pairs that share table- and column-level context through the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. They can describe business ownership, intended use, sensitivity, and other metadata, helping platforms, tools, and agents understand the data they access.

Databricks supports catalog labels through Tag Exchange, which exposes Unity Catalog’s table- and column-level tags through the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. External platforms, tools, and agents can use this context for discovery, classification, and locally defined access policies.

entries.title: What 5,400 Malicious npm Packages Reveal about Software Supply Chain Risk in 2026
entries.summary: Executive summaryThis report is the first of a series of blogs analyzing the supply chain threat landscape...
entries.content:
by Databricks Threat Research, Alessandra Rizzo , Panos Sakkos and Ariel Ropek

  • Hijacked real packages cause nearly all the exposure. Compromised legitimate packages are only 7% of the 5,400 malicious packages, but they account for over 99% of downloads.
  • Attackers have moved from stolen tokens to build pipelines. After npm revoked long-lived tokens, attackers took over CI environments and published through trusted publishing; 85% of trusted-published packages in the set are compromises.
  • AI development tools are a new target. Malicious MCP servers, packages that tamper with AI assistant configuration, and stealers of AI service keys are going after an attack surface that didn't exist two years ago.

This report is the first of a series of blogs analyzing the supply chain threat landscape. In this first part, we analyzed approximately 5,400 confirmed malicious npm packages published between December 2025 and October 2026, the first year following npm's revocation of long-lived authentication tokens [1]. Eight findings follow.

  1. Exposure is concentrated in compromised legitimate packages. Attacker-created malware packages constitute 89% of the set but 0.2% of its recorded downloads. Compromised legitimate packages constitute 7% of the set and over 99% of downloads.
  2. Install-script controls address roughly half of observed malware. 54% of packages declare a lifecycle script; the remainder execute on import or invocation. The largest campaign of the period, exceeding one thousand packages directed at a single organization, declared a lifecycle script in 1% of packages and alternated between import-time execution and postinstall hooks across successive waves.
  3. Account compromise has shifted from stolen tokens to compromised build pipelines. The highest-exposure victims of the August 2026 self-replicating worm campaign were republished through OIDC trusted publishing from compromised CI environments. Of packages in the set published via trusted publishing, 85% are compromised legitimate packages; attacker-created packages use trusted publishing in 0.1% of cases.
  4. Attacker infrastructure is predominantly legitimate shared services. 38% of malicious packages communicate with a legitimate third-party service: serverless hosting, chat-platform webhooks, code-hosting and paste sites, request-capture endpoints, and in a small number of cases public blockchain RPC nodes used as dead-drop resolvers. Domain reputation does not distinguish this traffic from normal developer traffic.
  5. A distinct class of activity targets AI development tooling. MCP server packages that harvest credentials from the agent host, packages that modify AI assistant configuration and instruction files, and credential stealers specialized in AI service keys together form a population whose principal targets, MCP hosts and assistant configuration, did not exist as an attack surface two years ago.
  6. Offensive-security frameworks marketed as AI agents are distributed through npm. Agentic offensive security frameworks have begun appearing on the registry for open source distribution, bundling remote-access, cloud-credential and enterprise-identity tooling with modules for adversarial testing of AI systems. Public reporting has already observed threat actors making use of agentic tooling against exposed secrets.
  7. The registry is used as a distribution channel for payloads unrelated to the software supply chain. The registry offers attackers free, highly available hosting under a trusted domain, and its content is redistributed by public CDNs and mirrors; victims who never run the package manager can therefore be served a payload directly from npm infrastructure.
  8. Removal is slower than reporting, and attackers remove their own packages faster than the registry does. 87% of confirmed packages have a public advisory; unattributed packages receive one at a median of 1.7 days after publication. The registry's security takedown follows at a median of 7 days, with 10% exceeding 59 days. 37% of attacker-created packages were unpublished by their own publisher, at a median of seven hours, before any takedown. 16% remained installable at the time of this analysis.

The dataset comprises packages detected by our scanner, which analyzes npm publish events for suspicious packages, with results filtered for precision by retaining only packages with at least one independent source: a public advisory, a vendor-published campaign report, an npm security takedown, or analyst review. Time is measured by npm publish date. The unit of record is the package version; a package is dated by its first malicious version. Download counts are monthly snapshots recorded at scan time. Registry active status was checked against the public registry on November 6, 2026.

Figure 1: Verdict Type by Month (%)

Monthly counts of confirmed malicious packages vary by a factor of fifteen across the period. The variation is attributable to a small number of campaigns: in August 2026 a single dependency-confusion campaign accounts for 78% of confirmed versions. When each campaign is counted as a single actor, activity is stable: several hundred new publisher accounts per month, a flat rate of malicious packages relative to total packages published, and spikes attributable to named campaigns.

Figure 2: Verified Malicious npm Packages by First-Publish Month

Three changes are observable after this normalization:

Compromise of legitimate packages is episodic. Activity is negligible in most months. Three waves of a single worm family occurred in May, June and August 2026; the May and August waves each compromised more than one hundred packages, and the June wave republished a vendor's entire scope in one day.

Figure 3: Legitimate-Package Compromise, Poisoned Versions by Month

Dependency-confusion reconnaissance is continuous, present in every month at a consistent level.

Obfuscation increased. The share of actors whose packages trigger an obfuscation rule more than doubled between May and August 2026.

Targeting of AI-developer credentials remained at 1-4% of packages throughout the year; absolute counts rose with volume. Theft of npm authentication tokens peaked at 22% of packages in March 2026 and fell below 5% from May. Classic long-lived tokens had been revoked on December 9, 2025; the tokens targeted in this period were plausibly granular access tokens and CI secrets.

Figure 4: Share of Verified Packages Targeting Each Credential Class, by Month

Figure 5: Cloud and AI-Dev Targeting: Packages vs. Actors (% of month)

Figure 6: Profiles of Verified Malicious npm Publishing, May–October 2026

Publisher account. 99% of malicious packages are published by single-maintainer accounts; 55% of accounts use a free-mail address. Two thirds of accounts publish exactly one malicious package; among accounts publishing more than one, the median interval from first to last malicious publish is under one day. DPRK-nexus campaigns are the exception, operating several hundred accounts at one to two packages each, 83% on free-mail addresses. Other named campaigns use free-mail addresses in 15% of cases, consistent with procured account pools.

Figure 7: Publisher accounts behind Verified Malicious npm Packages

Package metadata. 88% of packages are under thirty days old at the malicious publish; 75% declare no repository; 66% have a single version; 65% retain 

npm init
template values in the author, description or repository fields. 54% declare a lifecycle script. 17% carry an internal-looking name (core, utils, sdk, config). Typosquatting is a minority tactic: 13% embed a popular package name and under 5% are within two character edits of one.

Figure 8: Author and Repository Spoofing in package.json file (%)

Figure 9: Ecosystem Keywords Used in Malicious Package Names

Compromise indicators. Compromised legitimate packages differ from attacker-created packages on the version-level change signals. 78% of compromised versions add or modify a lifecycle script, compared with 4% of attacker-created packages. 23% show a change of maintainer or publisher. The majority of compromises are published through the legitimate account and leave ownership records unchanged.

Figure 10: Takeover Shape, Compromised Legitimate Packages vs Attacker-Published

Behavior. 72% of packages have an obfuscation marker, and 30% retrieve a second stage. Credential and data theft is the predominant behavior in every month, except August. A significant number of packages in August stole credentials but ultimately aimed to deliver on the victim machine a Sliver command-and-control implant, changing its classification to Trojan / Downloader.

Figure 11: Malware Packages by Behavior and Month

Of credential stealers, 45% target a single credential class and 36% target three or more. Single-class stealers are distributed evenly across cloud credentials, SSH keys, AI-developer credentials, npm tokens and 

.env
files. In multi-class stealers, cloud credentials, SSH keys and 
.env
files co-occur; wallet and browser-data theft occur separately. AI-developer credentials are the most specialized target: 80% of packages that target them target no other class.

Figure 12: Co-occurrence of credential classes

Platform. 55% of packages contain no operating-system-specific code. Among the remainder, droppers target Windows (PowerShell, scheduled tasks, executables) and credential stealers and backdoors target Linux (systemd, cron, shell configuration files). macOS-specific code appears in approximately one in eight stealers.

Figure 13: Targeted OS

Lures. 24% of packages are scoped, across more than three hundred distinct scopes, most of which contain a single malicious package: an organization's internal namespace registered once. 36% declare an author and 24% a repository; where present, approximately 80% of each refer to an identity other than the publishing account. 62% include a README; of these, 16% contain an installation command for a different package, in half of those cases a popular one. The majority of attacker-created packages employ no lure, consistent with the exposure finding: these packages are retrieved by misconfigured builds rather than selected by users.

Figure 14: Package-name lures (%)

Compromised legitimate packages are 7% of the set and over 99% of its download exposure.

Figure 15: Downloads per Month at Scan Time

All compromise waves in the period belong to one family, first the toolkit of a single threat actor and later open-sourced for free use in May. The May and August worms each compromised more than one hundred packages. In June 2026 the same open-source kit republished a single vendor's entire scope in one day through trusted publishing, followed within days by a small number of unrelated packages. Outside these waves, compromise occurs at a rate of a few packages per month.

Worm-compromised versions are distinguishable from attacker-created packages: all execute through a lifecycle script, one third read cloud credentials or the Kubernetes service-account token, and 44% trigger obfuscation rules. They receive public advisories within hours of publication.

The August wave's highest-exposure victims were republished through OIDC trusted publishing from compromised CI environments rather than through stolen tokens. Across the period, 85% of packages in the malicious set published via trusted publishing are compromises. The December 2025 token revocation directed maintainers toward trusted publishing; subsequent compromise activity targeted the publishing pipeline directly.

Shared legitimate services. 38% of packages, and 42% of those with a network indicator, communicate with a legitimate third-party service. Serverless hosting is most common; Cloudflare Workers alone serves several hundred packages from a comparable number of accounts. Code-hosting and paste sites follow, then Telegram, Discord and Slack webhooks. A small population retrieves its payload address from a smart contract via a public blockchain RPC endpoint; two thirds of these packages are heavily obfuscated and 42% ship a compiled binary. 8% of droppers carry no resolvable host, with the second-stage URL constructed at runtime.

Figure 16: Share of Packages Routing Through a Legitimate Service, by Month

Exposure. 81% of attacker-created packages had no downloads at the time of scanning. The ten most-downloaded packages in the set account for over 99% of recorded downloads; all are compromised legitimate packages.

Time to public advisory. 87% of the set has an OSV advisory. Named worm and dependency-confusion campaigns receive advisories on the day of publication. Unattributed packages receive advisories after a median of 1.7 days, with 10% exceeding one month. DPRK-nexus packages receive advisories after a median of 4.5 days, with 10% exceeding two months, the slowest of any developer-facing population.

Figure 17: Exposure Before Public Reporting

Registry outcome. Each attacker-created package was checked against the registry at the time of analysis. 40% had been replaced by npm's security placeholder, at a median of 7.1 days after publication and 10% after more than 59 days. 37% had been unpublished by their own publisher, at a median of 0.3 days; attackers withdraw packages faster than the registry removes them, and the share of self-removal rose through the year. 7% had been deleted without a recoverable timestamp. 16% remained installable. Removal rates vary by actor: 64% of DPRK-nexus packages were removed by npm, at a median lag of 19.5 days, and 5% remain installable; individual DPRK-nexus campaigns range from 16.4 to 65.9 days. Of unattributed packages, 21% remain installable. The registry takedown is a slower control than public reporting: from March 2026 onward the median advisory preceded the median takedown in every month.

Figure 18: Where Malicious Packages Ended Up

Figure 20: Days from Publish to Removal or Advisory, by Publish Month

Outcomes differ sharply by campaign. Campaigns that received same-day advisories had median takedown lags of a few days or less. DPRK-nexus campaigns received advisories within days but remained installable for weeks to months; every DPRK-nexus tag in the dataset has a median takedown lag above two weeks. A further group of campaigns, including five crypto-wallet stealer families, was never removed by the registry: the publishers withdrew every package themselves, typically within a day, and the registry recorded no security action.

  1. Install-script blocking is a partial control. It addresses the half of attacker-created packages that execute through a lifecycle script and all worm-compromised versions, and none of the packages that execute on import. Combine it with lockfile integrity enforcement and a registry proxy applying an allowlist or minimum-age policy.
  2. Monitor lifecycle-script changes between versions of existing dependencies. 78% of compromised versions add or modify a lifecycle script; 23% change maintainer or publisher.
  3. Restrict credentials available to build environments. One third of worm victims and half of MCP-abuse packages read cloud credentials. Short-lived, job-scoped credentials limit the impact.
  4. Treat trusted publishing as provenance, not assurance. It attests that a package originated from a pipeline, not that the pipeline was uncompromised. Pin CI actions, exclude secrets from pull-request builds, and review provenance attestations at publish time.
  5. Do not rely on domain reputation for build-time egress control. 38% of malicious packages communicate with Cloudflare, Vercel, GitHub, Telegram or public blockchain nodes. Egress policy must be allowlist-based.
  6. Register organizational scopes on the public registry. More than three hundred scopes were registered by attackers in the period, most once. Configure package managers to resolve internal scopes exclusively from internal registries.
  7. Protect AI assistant configuration as a credential store. Assistant configuration directories, MCP host configuration and instruction files are read and written by malicious packages. Apply file-integrity monitoring equivalent to that for SSH keys.
  8. Prepare for agent-operated intrusions. Autonomous offensive frameworks are now one npm install command away from a motivated actor. Plant content that trips an attacking agent's guardrails or diverts its plan, deploy canary credentials where an agent will enumerate them, and add agent-driven patterns to SOC detection: bursts of API calls with changing parameters, enumeration from one principal across many services, and credential use seconds after discovery.

This is the first in a series of posts on supply chain threats. In our next report, we will discuss emerging threats identified in the dataset that we believe are expanding the role of the npm registry beyond traditional malware distribution.

[1] GitHub (2025). “npm classic tokens revoked, session-based auth and CLI token management now available”.

entries.title: Announcing General Availability of native Lakebase Postgres sink for Spark Structured Streaming
entries.summary: Low-latency use cases like fraud detection, live personalization, and real-time feature...
entries.content:
Enable real-time feature computation and ingestion in a single streaming pipeline

by Navneeth Nair, David Young and Murali Talluri

  • Announcing General Availability of the native Lakebase sink for Apache Spark™ Structured Streaming: stream computed results directly into Lakebase with a single writeStream call, replacing custom foreach writers.
  • Learn how Real-Time Mode and the native Lakebase sink together enable real-time feature computation and ingestion into Lakebase in one streaming pipeline.
  • See it in action on a real-time feature pipeline, upserting ~20K EPS for 5 million users into Lakebase at p99 under 500 ms, end-to-end.

Low-latency use cases like fraud detection, live personalization, and real-time feature computation need computed results in a serving-ready OLTP store. Lakebase Postgres is Databricks' fully managed, serverless PostgreSQL database offering, with autoscaling, branching, native Unity Catalog integration, and sub 10ms reads. But writing to it from a streaming pipeline has meant building a custom 

foreach
writer and handling batching, retries, and upserts yourself, which is complex to get right and hard to keep performant under load.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of the native Lakebase sink for Apache Spark™ Structured Streaming, a connector that writes computed results directly to Lakebase and handles all of that for you. The same connector works in both micro-batch and Real-Time Mode. We show it on a feature pipeline that ingests watch and like events from a video streaming platform, computes each user's recent activity, and upserts one feature row per user into Lakebase in hundreds of milliseconds. You get that performance without building or maintaining the connector yourself.

A 

foreach
writer has to do a lot at once: batch writes for throughput, a bounded queue for backpressure, pool connections and refresh OAuth tokens, retry transient failures with backoff, deduplicate within a batch. It also has to implement upsert semantics correctly, including keeping the greatest timestamp or updating a column only when an incoming event has a newer ordering value.

Even for an experienced developer, writing and tuning all of this is weeks of work, and it does not end there. The connector turns into something you maintain, fixing throughput regressions, credential refresh, and keeping the code current with the latest versions. For a sense of what that looks like in practice, see this reference implementation. 

"We stream real-time data into Lakebase so our risk agent can pull a user's recent activity when it investigates an alert. We initially built that path with a custom ForeachWriter, which meant building and maintaining the write infrastructure ourselves. As part of our development work, we found that the native sink reduces the custom work required for connection pooling, batching, and retries." - Maria Marinova, Sr. Lead Software Engineer, DraftKings

The native sink takes care of it. You wire up a Lakebase write in minutes with a single 

writeStream
call, and spend no time on performance, tuning, or maintaining the connector. You get: 

  • Ease of use: no custom sink code; batching, connection reuse, and error handling are built in.
  • Upserts: declare an 
    upsertkey
    and the sink maintains one row per key.
  • Merge strategies for upserts: declarative custom merge logic for how non-key columns update on conflict. See supported merge strategies.
  • Reliable delivery: transient JDBC errors (connection failures, deadlocks, rate limiting) are retried automatically with exponential backoff.
  • A familiar API: the same 
    writeStream
    and 
    .toTable()
    used for Unity Catalog tables.
  • Tunable batching: optional caps on batch size and interval when the defaults don't fit your SLA.
  • UC-managed authentication: the connector authenticates to Lakebase automatically as the running user or service principal.
"Testing real-time data flows into Lakebase is an important part of validating how our risk agent can quickly access the freshest available user data when making decisions. As we evaluated the native sink, we found that its built-in connection pooling, batching, and retries reduce the custom infrastructure we need to build and maintain." - Georgi Stoychev, Sr. Software Automation Engineer, DraftKings

A video streaming provider wants to recommend videos to its viewers. A recommendation model needs what users watched most recently. So for each user we compute the last 6 videos they watched and the last 3 they liked. We store that as one row per user in Lakebase. At inference time, the recommendation model looks up that row by 

user_id
to rank what to show next.

A feature is an input the model uses to make a prediction. Here, the features are each user's recent activity, computed from a stream of events. Each event has a 

user_id
and a 
video_id
and an event type (WATCH/LIKE). For each user we keep their recent watches and likes as one row, keyed by 
user_id
. Every new event for a 
user_id
updates that row in place.

The pipeline is three stages:

  • Stream: read engagement events from Kafka.
  • Transform: group by 
    user_id
    and maintain each user's last-6 watched and last-3 liked with 
    transformWithState
    , emitting one feature row per user.
  • Write: upsert that row into Lakebase with the native sink.

Writing to Lakebase is a single 

writeStream
call. How you point it at Lakebase depends on whether the target table is registered in Unity Catalog.

If the Lakebase table is registered in Unity Catalog, write with 

.toTable()
using the fully qualified 
catalog.schema.table
. The connector manages credentials as the running user or service principal, and creates the table if it doesn't exist:

If the Lakebase table isn't registered in Unity Catalog, write to the Lakebase endpoint directly with 

format("postgresql")
(see Lakebase tables not registered with Unity Catalog). The same 
format("postgresql")
path also supports writing to external PostgreSQL databases (e.g. Amazon RDS or self-hosted) via a Unity Catalog connection (DBR 19+, Public Preview).

The sink writes the features into Lakebase within 100-200 milliseconds of being produced, with no offline-to-online sync in between. Applications and models can query them in single-digit milliseconds. This supports two patterns:

  • An application fetching a user's features by 
    user_id
    , a low-latency single-row lookup.
  • A model reads those same features for real-time inference, so its predictions reflect what the users just did.

For a deeper look at the implementation, see the companion repo, a self-serve example you can run end-to-end.

We ran the pipeline at a sustained input rate of ~20K events/sec against 5 million active users, each accumulating watch and like history. The cluster used was a 40-core classic compute (DBR 18 LTS) writing to an 8-CU Lakebase project with 5-minute RTM checkpoint intervals.

Every event is an upsert that overwrites that user's existing feature row in Lakebase. As state builds up, the sink is continuously upserting against a table with millions of existing rows, finding and replacing the row for each 

user_id
on every event. This is the workload pattern that breaks custom 
foreach
 writers at scale.

End-to-end latency is measured from the Kafka input timestamp to the row landing in Lakebase.

These latencies are specific to this setup. Your numbers will differ with input rate, the amount of state you keep, RTM cluster size, and Lakebase size. Size both the cluster and Lakebase to sustain the throughput you need. The sink also lets you tune how it batches writes using 

batchinterval
and 
batchsize
. See performance tuning.

At this throughput on an 8-CU project, 

pg_stat_statements
shows 63.5 million upserts averaging ~0.015 milliseconds per statement. Lakebase had headroom to spare. For a deeper look at how Lakebase achieves this, see the blog, How Lakebase Architecture Delivers 5x Faster Postgres Writes.

With Real-Time Mode computing features as events arrive and the native Lakebase sink enabling writes directly to a serving-ready OLTP database, together they unblock real-time feature computation and ingestion in one streaming pipeline.

The native sink gives you a first-class experience when writing to Lakebase, using the same 

writeStream
API you already know. We showed it on a recommendation feature pipeline, but the same pattern works wherever a streaming pipeline needs to write computed results to a database for immediate serving.

The native Lakebase sink for Spark Structured Streaming is now Generally Available.

  • Companion repo: run the full feature pipeline end-to-end in your workspace.
  • Write to Lakebase from Structured Streaming: sink configuration, supported triggers, output modes, and tuning options.
  • Lakebase Postgres: instance setup, UC integration, and serving.

What is the native Lakebase sink for Spark Structured Streaming?

It’s a Structured Streaming connector that writes computed results directly to Lakebase. It handles batching, retries, connection pooling, deduplication, upserts, and workspace-managed authentication, so you don’t build a custom 

foreach
writer. The same connector works in both micro-batch and Real-Time Mode.

Is the native Lakebase sink generally available?

Yes. The native Lakebase sink for Spark Structured Streaming is now generally available on Databricks Runtime 18 LTS and above. The RealTime and ProcessingTime triggers run on classic compute; on serverless, use 

Trigger.AvailableNow
. It isn’t supported in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines.

How do I write to Lakebase with the sink?

For a Lakebase table registered in Unity Catalog, use 

.toTable()
with the fully qualified 
catalog.schema.table
; the connector manages credentials and creates the table if it doesn’t exist. For an unregistered table, use 
format("postgresql")
with the Lakebase 
endpoint
and 
dbtable
.

Does the sink support upserts and custom merge logic?

Yes. Declare an 

upsertkey
and the sink maintains one row per key. Merge strategies (DBR 19+) control how non-key columns update on conflict, such as keeping the latest non-null value or the value from the newest event, with no hand-written 
ON CONFLICT
SQL.

What use cases is the native Lakebase sink built for?

The native Lakebase sink is built for operational dashboards, app databases, and low-latency feature stores.. Examples include real-time feature computation for recommendations and personalization, and fraud detection.

entries.summary: Why we built itMost Databricks architecture talks used to start with the same slide: ingestion on the left...
entries.content:
How we replaced our static standard reference architecture slides with an interactive architecture board across 70 industries, for 3 clouds in 16 languages augmented with product regional availability and learning materials.

by Ashraf Osman, Amr Ali and Shelley Shaffery

  • Start from your industry. Pick one of 70 industries and a cloud and the board shows the source systems, teams, use cases, and Databricks products that go with it.
  • See what runs in your region. Pick a region and get the list of products and features available there, with each one's release stage and a link to the docs that say so.
  • Take it into your next meeting. Export the board as a PowerPoint or PDF deck, an image, or an editable draw.io, Visio, or Excalidraw file, in any of 16 languages.

Most Databricks architecture talks used to start with the same slide: ingestion on the left, the lakehouse in the middle, BI and AI on the right. The slide is correct, but it doesn't specify where a bank's core banking ledger and SWIFT payment messages go. A hospital wants to know what happens to the HL7 messages from its electronic health record (EHR) system and to its DICOM medical images. A utility asks about smart meter reads and the SCADA data coming off the grid.

So people redrew the slide for each industry, and the copies drifted apart. They went out of date with every product release, lived on individual laptops, and there was no way to tell which one was current.

The Databricks Reference Architecture simplifies this journey. It's a public, interactive board with a version for each of the 70 industries, updated from the Databricks docs, so it doesn't go stale. Every box opens a panel with what it is, who uses it, and where to learn more. You can also copy any board and change it to fit your own systems.

The architecture board covers 70 industries across 11 economic sectors as of November 16th 2026. Click a name to open its board.

You'll find the same list in the industry picker at the top of the board. You can search for any industry of interest and interact with it. There is also the Standard Reference Architecture, which is the architecture board with no industry bias.

The Databricks Platform in the middle is the same across industries. What changes are the things surrounding it.

The sources are the systems that industry actually runs: 964 different ones across the 70 boards as of the release of this blog. They're grouped the way people in that sector talk about them. Like EHR, imaging, and revenue cycle in healthcare, or metering, SCADA, and outage management at a utility. Most source boxes also specify what data they send: whether it's batch or streaming, its shape, how much, and how often. By default, a source shows its type, such as Electronic Health Record (EHR). Switch to Branded to see the vendor products instead.

The boards also list the data formats each industry exchanges, 186 in all. They run from FIX and ISO 20022 in finance to HL7, FHIR and DICOM in healthcare and OPC UA in manufacturing, and each one links to the body that publishes it.

The teams carry the names each sector uses, like Treasury and ALM at a bank or Grid Operations at a utility, with 1,538 personas across the 70 boards.

The medallion layers use the industry's own terms too. On the banking board, Gold holds net interest margin and liquidity ratios. On the healthcare board, it holds length of stay and patient outcomes. And every board has 10 use cases, 4 Genie Agents, 4 AI/BI Dashboards, and 4 Databricks Apps written for that industry.

Here's how six of them compare, from the sources to the Silver layer:

Industry Source system groups Data formats Conformed in Silver
Banking Core banking, cards and payments, digital channels, risk and finance, open banking ISO 20022, SWIFT MT, BAI2, Nacha ACH Customers and accounts
Healthcare EHR and clinical, revenue cycle, imaging and devices, operations and staffing HL7 v2, FHIR, DICOM, X12N Patients and encounters
Manufacturing ERP and planning, MES and shop floor, quality and PLM, IoT and historians OPC UA, MTConnect, B2MML, Sparkplug Orders and lots
Telecommunications BSS and billing, OSS and inventory, customer care, field service, fraud and assurance CDR, TAP3, NRTRDE, TMF Open APIs Subscribers and sessions
Electric utility Metering and AMI, SCADA and grid operations, customer and billing, GIS and outage management CIM, IEC 61850, DNP3, COMTRADE Meters and premises
Pharmaceuticals Discovery and R&D, clinical and EDC, GxP manufacturing, quality and LIMS, safety and commercial eCTD, ICH E2B(R3), SPL, CDISC Subjects and batches

Every board opens in Simplified. It shows what you need to read the industry: the first entries in each group, key systems like a bank's core banking system, the use cases with Databricks customer stories, and the core cloud services.

Detailed view adds everything else such as CI/CD, monitoring, and operational stores, along with captions, capability tags, and descriptions. Switch views in the toolbar. Shared links and exports follow the view on screen.

All 700 use cases say what problem they solve, which team benefits, and how they're built on Databricks, with a link to every product they use. 581 of them link to at least one Databricks customer story and those are listed first. When there's a Databricks Solution Accelerator for a use case the panel links to it so that you can start from working code.

Genie Agents work the same way. On the pharmaceuticals board, the Trial Enrollment Agent reads the electronic data capture and clinical trial management systems for the clinical operations team, biopharma leaders, and clinical trial managers. Its panel lists the questions those teams would ask it, such as which sites are under-enrolling this month.

Click a team to see the people in it, the use cases they own, and the Databricks products they use, with a line on what each product is for. The panel also builds a learning path for that team from free Databricks Academy courses and certifications, adds the customer stories, demos, and videos that matter to them.

The medallion layers link to a deployable data model. Open Silver on the banking board and the panel links to the banking model in the Databricks Industry Data Models, with its tables and columns. We introduced those models in Jumpstart your Data Modeling with Databricks Industry Data Models, and the agent that builds them in Reimagining Data Modeling on the Lakehouse: Introducing Vibe Data Modeling.

Source boxes go one level down, into the data itself. The process historian on the manufacturing board collects sensor tags from the production lines. Its panel says who uses that data and how much of it arrives, a continuous stream of 10,000 to 100,000 tags a second.

This is the part we use most. Before anyone designs anything, two questions come up: does the product run in the region where we deploy and is it GA or still in preview?

Pick a region from the Region menu. The board dims every product that region can't run and a panel opens with the full list for that region. It lists every product and feature that the Databricks docs publish, along with their release stage and whether they're available there. When the docs add a note, such as a feature that processes data outside your geography, the panel shows it too. Each row links to the docs page it came from.

The list filters like a spreadsheet. Untick GA in the Stage column and you're left with what's in Public Preview or Beta. You can also sort it, search it, and download it to Excel. The address bar keeps your filters, so you can send someone exactly the view you're looking at.

If you only want to clean up the board itself, the Stage menu filters the platform by release stage. Turn off Beta and the previews and everything that isn't GA drops out of the picture. That's handy when you need a GA-only architecture for a review.

Both the stages and the regions come from the public Databricks documentation. We refresh them before every change to the board and the board shows the date of the last refresh.

Every board works on Azure, AWS, and GCP. Switch the cloud, ingestion tools change with it, and the docs links point to that cloud's documentation.

The boards are translated into 16 languages, laid out right-to-left for Arabic and Hebrew and the exports are in the language you're reading.

Every industry also has its own share link and preview card. Post the link in Slack, Teams, or LinkedIn and it opens on that industry, with its name on the card.

Any board exports as a PowerPoint or PDF deck with a contents page, the board, and a page for each use case, Genie Agent, dashboard, and app. In the PowerPoint, the board slide is built from real shapes so that you can move and relabel the boxes. The board also downloads as a PNG, an animated GIF, interactive HTML, an editable draw.io file, a Visio file, a SVG file, an Excalidraw file, or a YAML file you can edit and import back.

If you'd rather start from a description the AI Architecture Assistant finds the closest industry for you. Describe the business or attach a whiteboard photo or a PDF and it builds an editable architecture from that industry's board. It runs as a Databricks App in your own workspace and the repository also includes an MCP server that gives AI agents all 70 architectures.

Treat an industry board as a starting point. Every company has its own systems, constraints, and history. A sub-vertical can look quite different from its parent industry. Vendor products change too. If you spot something out of date, tell us through the Feedback button.

Open the Databricks Reference Architecture, pick your industry and cloud and click any box. The code and an installer for your own workspace are on GitHub. If your industry is missing or a board makes a mistake, use the Feedback button at the top of the board.

We're building pipelines that update the board as products ship, instead of waiting for the next change to the repository.

Explore the interactive reference architecture

What is a Databricks reference architecture?

A free, interactive board that shows how Databricks fits a specific industry: the source systems, data formats, teams, use cases and products involved. There's a version for each of 70 industries, and you can export or edit any of them.

Is it free?

Yes. The board is public and free to use, and the code and an installer for your own workspace are on GitHub.

Which clouds and regions does it cover?

Every board works on AWS, GCP and Azure Cloud. Pick a region to see which products and features are available there, and their release stage, straight from the Databricks docs.

Can I tailor a board to my own environment?

Yes. Use Download to copy an industry board then customize using the tool of your choice. You can also edit and re-import a YAML file.

How can I tell which products are available in my region or release stage?

Choose a region to see products that are unavailable there, and use the release-stage filter to check availability stages such as GA, public preview, and beta. Product panels link to the relevant documentation.

How current is the product and regional availability information?

Availability information is checked against public Databricks documentation before board updates. Automated update pipelines are planned, so updates are not yet described as live.

Can I use the reference architecture on a different cloud or in another language?

Yes. The boards support Azure, AWS, and GCP, and are available in 16 languages, including right-to-left layouts for Arabic and Hebrew.

Can I run the reference architecture in my own workspace?

Yes. The source code and an installer are available on GitHub for setting it up in your workspace.

How do I report an error or request an industry that is not listed?

Use the Feedback button at the top of the board to report an issue or request an additional industry.

entries.title: Why PostgreSQL 19 shipped late
entries.summary: PostgreSQL 19 is now generally available, and there are some really cool things in...
entries.content:
AI made bugs much easier to find, but fixing them still takes humans

by Jonathan Katz and Robert Haas

  • PostgreSQL 19 shipped about a month after the usual September to October window for major PostgreSQL releases. The delay came from the project's focus on quality.
  • Starting around February 2026, AI made bugs and security issues far easier to find. CVEs fixed per quarterly update release went from one to four up to 28 by August 2026, and commits back-patched to the release branch rose 61%.
  • Contributors spent time fixing those bugs that would have gone into reviewing new features. The project is adapting, and AI scrutiny is a chance to make PostgreSQL better than it's ever been.

PostgreSQL 19 is now generally available, and there are some really cool things in it:

  • REPACK rebuilds bloated tables while normal reads and writes continue
  • Query plan advice lets you stabilize the plan for a critical query without changing application SQL
  • WAIT FOR LSN gives you read-your-writes on replicas without polling or arbitrary sleeps
  • Logical replication can now synchronize sequences, which removes a common migration headache

We walked you through what's new on PostgreSQL 19 here. In this post, we take a step back; as PostgreSQL contributors, we want to share some backstory on how a major release comes together, and some reflections on PostgreSQL 19 and what made this release different.

Over the past decade, the timing of PostgreSQL major releases has become very predictable: no earlier than the middle of September, and no later than the middle of October. This year was different: PostgreSQL 19 shipped more than a month after that window closed. So, what happened?

To answer that, it helps to know what a normal year looks like.

PostgreSQL started in the 1980s as the POSTGRES project at UC Berkeley, and it has been developed in the open since 1996. No single company owns it. A worldwide community of developers builds it, and that community values reliability and predictability. Part of that predictability is the calendar: one major release a year, at about the same time each year.

Each release takes 14 to 15 months from the first commits to general availability, and that time splits into two phases:

  • Development: there are five commitfests - in July, September, November, January, and March/April - each focused on reviewing and committing patches. Feature freeze follows the last one, in April.
  • Stabilization
    • Beta 1 typically ships in May
    • The release branch is cut in June, around Beta 2 - this also opens up new development on the next release
    • Beta 3 follows in August
    • There’s a release candidate in September
    • General availability happens late September or October

When a feature can't be stabilized in time, the usual practice is to defer it to a future major version and keep the release on schedule.

All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL's code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There's a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs.

That's always been true, and it hasn't stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What's different now is that it's become vastly easier to find those bugs. Fixing them has also gotten easier, but not to the same degree.

The change came quickly. Around February 2026, developers started noticing that the latest models were good enough to write real code, that the code going to production wasn't as buggy, and that the models were helping them move faster.

Reviewing code and researching security issues used to take a lot of human expertise. With AI, they take much less, and how much AI can discover on its own has gone up sharply.

You can see the result in PostgreSQL's quarterly update releases. From August 2023 through November 2025, each one fixed between one and four CVEs. In 2026, that went to 5 in February, 11 in May, and 28 in August. Bug fixes per update release followed the same curve, from roughly 50 to 75 per release to about 140 in August 2026.

Not every CVE is equally severe though. Many of the bug fixes are long-tail issues. But the volume is still higher than we’re used to.

The commit history shows the same thing. Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL's master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE. In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%.

It's possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but that’s unlikely. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years, but a lot more of the mistakes they made were quickly found by LLMs.

And it isn't just mistakes in the latest release. In the same time period, during 2025, there were 248 commits to REL_17_STABLE, and during 2026, there were 433 commits to REL_18_STABLE. In other words, the number of commits being back-patched not just to the release in progress but also to at least one prior release jumped by more than 74% in a single year.

The reason for this is simply that a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very busy fixing them.

Time that would have gone into reviewing what was going into PostgreSQL 19 went into fixing security issues and other bugs in the back branches instead. A few features that were in progress this cycle weren't ready in time, so the project did what it always does and deferred them to a future release.

The fixes kept coming right up to the end. The November 12 update release for the supported branches included so many fixes that the release team put out a second release candidate so PostgreSQL 19 could ship with them.

In the end, we got PostgreSQL 19 out the door, a few weeks later than usual, and the delay came directly from the project's concern for quality. The way we all develop software has changed, and the PostgreSQL community is adapting.

Nobody knows yet exactly how open source software development will change, but contributors across the PostgreSQL project are working hard to figure it out. LLMs are going to push every PostgreSQL developer, and to some extent every software developer, to raise their game. Every feature we write from now on will be scrutinized by AI, and bugs that would have gone unnoticed forever in an earlier era will now be found, sometimes in a matter of hours.

That's a big challenge, and an even bigger opportunity to make PostgreSQL better than it's ever been. We're excited to be part of it.

entries.title: Genie ZeroOps, now in public beta: An autonomous agent that fixes data pipelines, with lessons from 80,000 customer issues
entries.summary: In June we introduced Genie ZeroOps, an autonomous agent that detects, investigates,...
entries.content:
Over half of the pipeline issues we saw needed company-specific knowledge to fix. So we built shared inboxes, custom agent instructions, and one-click PRs to help data teams triage faster.

by Jeff Chou, Kristóf Molnár, Lennart Kats, Danny Chiao and Ray Zhu

  • Genie ZeroOps is built and refined from observations across over 80,000 customer pipeline issues.
  • Direct access to Unity Catalog, metadata, and pipeline lineage powers its autonomous resolution engine.
  • New team collaboration and one-click PR capabilities are now live for any workspace to enable in open beta.

In June we introduced Genie ZeroOps, an autonomous agent that detects, investigates, and resolves data pipeline issues, such as upstream schema changes or data quality anomalies. Based on extensive private preview testing with hundreds of customers, we’ve added new features to help data teams triage issues faster - including inbox sharing, notifications, one-click PR creation, and the ability to add custom business instructions to follow specific company workflows. Today, Genie ZeroOps is available in Public Beta, and your workspace admin can turn it on from the workspace Previews page.

Data engineering teams are underwater, managing many thousands of pipelines a day. Some pipeline failures are easy to find and fix - a job fails, a pipeline update errors out, and someone gets paged. Others are silent - a table stops updating, or last night's load arrives with half its usual rows, and nobody notices until a dashboard shows the wrong number.

Either way, the work that follows typically looks the same: a notification is sent, an engineer spends the next few hours manually investigating logs, upstream tables, and related assets, and finally a PR gets generated with the fix.

Genie ZeroOps automates this entire manual workflow while maintaining security, governance, and recommendation quality, specifically guiding teams from initial issue alert to a pull request across five core steps:

  • Detect: Continuously monitor jobs, pipelines, and tables for failures. Detect both hard job failures with jobs monitoring and silent data freshness and completeness issues with data quality monitoring.
  • Investigate: Gather context across logs, source code, table metadata, and lineage. Run SQL queries to pinpoint root causes, recommend fixes, and prioritize insights by downstream impact.
  • Verify: Test proposed fixes using unit tests and dry runs in a sandbox to safely validate hypotheses before applying changes.
  • Notify: Send alerts to Slack, Teams, or PagerDuty with a summary of the issue and recommended fix. Filter out low priority issues to help teams focus on urgent matters.
  • Remediate: Propose a code fix, and for Git-backed Jobs, automatically create a PR with pre-populated details.

During the limited private preview, ZeroOps observed over 80,000 real customer issues across hundreds of companies, highlighting just how painful pipeline maintenance has become. We found that over half of issues require organization-specific knowledge to properly triage, rank, and resolve, which speaks to the fundamental need for custom context. Through this feedback, we identified and built several critical features every team needs to succeed with ZeroOps:

  • Shared inbox: Pipeline management is a team sport. Share your ZeroOps inbox with your team, so everyone sees the same incidents eliminating gaps in coverage
  • Notifications with summaries: ZeroOps sends alerts with a brief summary of the issue and recommendation for each new insight so users can make informed decisions instantly. Filter notifications via custom instructions to keep noise down.
  • Custom agent instructions: Every team runs pipelines differently and needs to steer recommendations to follow their own business rules. Add custom instructions, such as known flaky sources, preferred fixes, or naming conventions, so ZeroOps recommendations reflect how your team works with the context it needs.
  • 1-click PR creation: Move from diagnosis to resolution in one click. ZeroOps automatically generates a pull request with code fixes and details pre-populated.
  • Governance built in: ZeroOps follows your existing Unity Catalog permissions, so it sees only what it's allowed to, and shared insights follow the same rules. PII is redacted before any notification leaves Databricks.

During our private preview, we spoke with customers who were prototyping internal AI triage tools. We learned that while building a simple prototype has become easier, scaling automated triage across production environments introduces complex operational challenges that compound over time:

  • System maintenance: Monitoring a system that manages thousands of pipelines across multiple teams requires constant upkeep, tracking service level agreements, and coordinating notifications among diverse stakeholders.
  • Governance and security: Effective triage requires access to source repositories, data tables, and internal tooling. Safely configuring user and agent access levels across these systems at scale is a significant challenge.
  • Custom context expansion: Actionable AI recommendations require custom context like documentation, tribal knowledge, and historical behaviors. Ingesting, expanding, and managing this context is difficult to scale.
  • Accuracy and drift: Context bloat can lead to hallucinations or reduced accuracy over time. Maintaining evaluation suites and monitoring recommendation quality requires ongoing engineering investment.

Genie ZeroOps handles these complexities natively - leveraging direct access to your Unity Catalog, metadata, and pipeline lineage to resolve issues with full context.

Try ZeroOps out for yourself! Have a workspace admin enable the ZeroOps feature. Then find the ZeroOps banner on the top of the pipelines page:

Read the documentation here for more details on how to get started.

If your team needs help onboarding ZeroOps to production, reach out to your account team to inquire about any workshops that we offer.

No, ZeroOps will never change your code or data without your direct approval. Today, it investigates the failure, proposes a fix and can push that fix to a new branch for a pull request. It never changes production code or data without a person reviewing it first.

It uses Data Quality Monitoring to flag tables whose commits arrive unusually late (freshness) or whose row counts fall below the expected range (completeness).

ZeroOps automatically triggers as soon as an issue is detected, without a prompt, so the analysis is ready before anyone looks. It also has built-in access to run history, Unity Catalog lineage, Delta history and DQM signals, and it works within your Unity Catalog permissions.

From the documentation, It reads run logs, source code, upstream table metadata and samples, while respecting Unity Catalog permissions. It uses models hosted by Databricks inside our security perimeter. Model calls stay in your workspace's region, and the model provider doesn't retain prompts or responses.

Yes. Add a custom instruction to filter out unwanted notifications, or mark an insight as "not an issue."
