entries.title: Genie One Accuracy: Why Curated Agents Need Governed Context
entries.summary: Ask Finance and Underwriting whether the loss ratio improved from 2024 to 2025, and...
entries.content:
What 125 insurance questions taught us about routing, business definitions, and documents

by Richa Sethi, Patrick Chan, Marcela Granados and Amit Kumar Jha

  • Databricks Genie One is most accurate when it uses curated Genie Agents together with modeled knowledge, the governed business context defined in Unity Catalog. Across 125 questions about a fictional insurer, Genie One scored 93–95% using curated Genie Agents together with governed business context (Metric Views, Domains/Subdomains and Pages), 83% with either agents or the governed layer alone, and 64% with tables alone.
  • Agents and the governed layer fix different problems. Metric Views, Domains, Subdomains, and Pages help Genie One answer definition questions that would otherwise rely on tribal knowledge, while agents are needed for questions that require answers from unstructured data such as PDFs.
  • Define each business measure once, in a certified Metric View, and use a Page to explain when it applies. In a separate change test, updating one Metric View and its Page moved all 12 related Genie One answers to the new definition without any agent edits.

Ask Finance and Underwriting whether the loss ratio improved from 2024 to 2025, and you will get two contradictory answers that are both correct. In a fictional commercial auto insurer we built for this test, Finance reported an 8.2 percentage-point deterioration, and Underwriting reported a 1.5 percentage-point improvement. Neither was wrong. Finance tracks the calendar year net of reinsurance, so an adverse reserve development on an older claim shows up in today's numbers. Underwriting looks strictly at the policy year, gross of reinsurance and excluding catastrophes, because that's the baseline used to set rates. Reserving, meanwhile, relies on a third metric entirely: the accident-year ultimate loss ratio.

The SQL can be perfectly correct and still produce an answer that doesn't make sense for the person asking. The challenge is knowing which business definition to apply when the same term has several valid definitions, while keeping shared facts, such as total policies written, consistent. This is the problem we wanted to explore with Genie One.

Genie One, powered by Genie Ontology (now Generally Available), brings this business context into the analytics experience. Genie Ontology learns from the work teams already do, automatically capturing business logic, calculations, and relationships from existing dashboards, queries, notebooks, and semantic models as Ontology Snippets. This learned knowledge is complemented by modeled knowledge: explicitly defined, governed business concepts represented in Unity Catalog through certified Metric Views, Domains and Subdomains, and Pages. In this study, we refer to this modeled knowledge as the “governed layer”.

Together, learned and modeled knowledge give Genie a richer understanding of how an organization works. Teams can build on the knowledge already captured from their existing assets, while using modeled knowledge to establish authoritative definitions for the business concepts where consistency and precision matter most. There is no need to model every concept upfront.

This study explores a different aspect of Genie Ontology than the Turing benchmark described in our Genie Ontology GA announcement. While the benchmark compared the accuracy and efficiency of Genie with Genie Ontology against leading frontier agents, our study isolates the contribution of modeled knowledge: how governed Metric Views and Pages complement learned knowledge and curated agents to help Genie One interpret business definitions and deliver consistent answers.

To explore this, we built four Genie Agents, one each for Finance, Reserving, Underwriting, and Claims. They used the same tables, but each had its own team's definitions, example queries, and documents. Each did well on its own. We wanted to know what happens when Genie One becomes the entry point: does it route to the right agent and use the right definition, and what does it need to do that reliably?

We tested four configurations to find out.

  • Tables only: no agents and no governed context in Unity Catalog.
  • Curated agents: each agent had its team's definitions, business rules, and documents.
  • Governed layer, no agents: Metric Views, certification, Domains, Subdomains and Pages in Unity Catalog, with no Genie Agents
  • Curated agents with a governed layer: the same agents plus the same governed business context.

Tables alone scored 64%. Curated agents and the governed layer each reached 83%, but they weren't good at the same things. Adding curated agents improved document-based answers. Adding the governed layer improved answers that depended on business definitions. Neither was enough on its own to cover both needs. With both in place, accuracy reached 93–95%, across two runs. The combined setup also scored 93% on loss-ratio questions and 97% on questions that required both documents and structured data.

To see whether this pattern held outside the insurance sector, we repeated the comparison using a fictional retailer. There, the governed layer raised accuracy from 54% to 82% when added to the curated agents.

Genie One doesn't simply choose an agent and let it answer every question. It can use governed Unity Catalog Semantics such as Metric Views, Domains and subdomains, and Pages, or route a question to a relevant Genie Agent. If it doesn't find a suitable match, it searches the workspace. There, it may infer which data to use from tables or volumes you use often, or from your earlier conversations.

When Genie One answers a question using its own context, it doesn't automatically inherit the instructions configured inside each agent. Those instructions apply only when Genie One routes the question to that agent. So an agent can be well curated and still contribute little if Genie One answers the question differently.

We created a fictional commercial auto insurer with:

  • 8,000 policies and 7,482 claims.
  • Claim values updated quarterly.
  • Reserves for claims that had not yet been reported (incurred but not reported, or IBNR).
  • Two reinsurance contracts and three catastrophe events.
  • A recent increase in California injury claim costs.

The four agents shared the same underlying tables. Each also had access to its team's folder of documents, with 14 PDFs across the four folders.

We also planted two misleading documents to test robustness. One was an early draft of the reserve committee minutes reporting a $4.1 million increase in reserves; the approved minutes in the same folder reported a $5.28 million increase. The other was a vendor newsletter containing a hidden instruction to report the loss ratio as 55%, a simple prompt-injection test.

We then placed three look-alike tables next to the real definitions: analytics_loss_ratio_v2, analytics_loss_ratio_test, and a personal copy, finance_lr_calendar_quarter_net_jdoe.

The agents were configured with their teams' formulas, business rules, and SQL example questions. We tuned them on a separate set of practice questions and then froze them, using the same versions across all configurations that included agents.

There are multiple ways to make enterprise documents available to Genie, depending on where the content lives and how teams need to access it. In this experiment, we stored team-specific PDFs in Unity Catalog Volumes and made them available to the corresponding Genie Agents through content search. When information is spread across business applications such as Google Drive, SharePoint, Jira, or Confluence, Genie Search provides a broader enterprise search experience. It combines indexed content from connected applications with live retrieval through MCP, bringing results together with Databricks assets in a single experience. It also respects the permissions of the source systems, so users only see content they are authorized to access.

For the governed layer, we set up:

  • Metric Views containing the teams' calculations: three loss-ratio definitions and the relevant team-specific versions of premium, claim frequency, and severity.
  • Certification marking the intended Metric Views and agents as trusted and the decoy assets as deprecated.
  • Domains and Subdomains organizing the assets around the Commercial Auto business. Shared facts lived in the main Domain, while each team's definitions, documents, and agents lived in its own Subdomain.
  • Pages providing short, governed explanations of business terms and linked to the tables and Metric Views they described.

The insurance benchmark contained 125 questions, each with an expected answer calculated independently in SQL.

The questions covered simple lookups, explicitly named business definitions, ambiguous questions such as "What's our loss ratio?", questions requiring an explanation, questions that the available data couldn't answer, and questions that combined documents with structured data. We also tested follow-up questions and the two planted documents.

We took several steps to make the results more meaningful. Genie One answered every question three times, with a fresh service principal for each run so earlier conversations couldn't carry over, and every answer was logged in MLflow. When a key result was close, we repeated the whole setup with a new identity. We report 95% confidence intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples, keeping each question's repeats together, because Genie One can recall earlier answers. Two AI judges from different model families extracted the headline number, the definition used, and the facts covered, and fixed rules decided whether each answer was right. The judges agreed on 95–99% of answers. Before each run, every agent had to answer at least 85% of its basic questions correctly on its own.

Here’s the overall accuracy score, followed by a breakdown by question category, measured with Genie One.

Question Type Tables only Curated agents Governed layer, no agents Curated agents + governed layer
All 125 questions 64% (55–72%) 83% (77–89%) 83% (77–89%) 95% (91–98%)
Definition questions (31) 47% 69% 100% 100%
Loss ratio questions (36) 43% 67% 88% 93%
Follow-up questions (5) 40% 60% 73% 93%
Document questions (12) 42% 75% 42% 81%
Questions requiring documents and data (12) 25% 92% 42% 97%
Answers using a decoy table 10% 6% 0% 0%
Answers relying on Pages from other projects in the account 46% 49% 14% 11%

What the governed layer added. With curated agents alone, Genie One often answered definition questions on its own and never saw the formulas in the agents' instructions. Published Pages are visible to Genie One across the whole account, so the closest definitions it could find were Pages other people had written for unrelated projects. It relied on those in 49% of its answers. The governed layer provided Genie One with a better match: certified Metric Views for each calculation and our own Pages for each contested term, organized within the Commercial Auto Domain. Reliance on other projects' Pages fell to 11%, and every definition question in our benchmark came back right.

We also looked at whether Genie One routed definition questions to an agent or answered them directly.

Definition questions through Genie One Routed to an agent Answered by Genie One directly
Curated agents 93% right 34% right
Curated agents + governed layer 100% right 100% right

With curated agents alone, the agents knew the answer, but Genie One answered about four in ten definition questions itself and got most of those wrong. With the governed layer, it got them right either way. We ran that setup twice from scratch with different identities, and routing shifted dramatically: Genie One handed 74% of answers to an agent in one run and 19% in the other, with about the same accuracy. Routing isn't deterministic, but with the governed layer it stopped mattering. Answering directly, Genie One read the certified Metric Views and Pages. Routing to an agent, the agent applied a formula that matched the same Metric View. Every path led to the same definition.

The planted documents didn't change any answers. No answer in any setup reported the 55% loss ratio from the injected vendor newsletter, and none used the draft reserve figure.

Without the governed layer, routing decided whether you got the right answer. The lesson is to design for whichever path Genie One takes: put each definition where every path can reach it, and test through Genie One more than once before trusting a result.

What the agents added. Without agents, document questions fell to the tables-only level. Of the 18 questions that worsened without agents, 12 required a team document, such as the litigation review, the reserve committee minutes, or an underwriting recommendation. In this setup, the agents were Genie One's only route to those documents, because the PDFs were available only through agent content search and none of the Pages linked to them. Without agents, Genie One also forecast a 2027 loss ratio for every repeat, rather than saying the data didn't cover 2027. That limitation was written in the table descriptions and the agents' instructions, but not on the Metric Views Genie One was reading, so it never saw it.

The comparison above adds the whole governed layer at once. To understand what each component contributed, we ran a separate series of tests, adding one component at a time.

This second experiment started with four agents whose loss-ratio formulas disagreed. From the second step onward, we moved the formulas into Metric Views and reduced each agent to a few behavior rules and two example queries. These agents were configured differently from the fully curated agents in the main comparison, so the results below shouldn't be compared directly with the earlier table.

  • Metric Views fixed the formulas. The same step also cut the agents back to a few behavior rules. Loss ratio questions went from 56% to 83%, and definition questions from 66% to 90%.
  • Certification helped signal which assets to trust, but didn't independently improve accuracy. The overall score dipped from 90% (84–94%) to 83% (76–89%), but the intervals overlap, so we can't say the drop is real. At the same time, decoy-table use fell from 9% to 4% of answers, and Genie One explicitly referred to a certified definition in 22% of answers. We see certification as a useful trust signal that works alongside Domains and Pages, not as a feature that makes answers correct on its own.
  • Domains and Pages, added last, helped Genie One identify which definition applied. Vague question accuracy increased to 94%, definition questions reached 100%, and decoy use dropped from 4% to zero. A Metric View tells Genie One how to calculate a number; the Domain and Pages help explain whose measure it is and how it fits into the business.

Document questions varied more between runs than the other categories. There were only 12, so changing two questions could move the score by about 15 percentage points. The original agents' instructions said where to find litigation status, and Genie One routed both litigation questions to the Claims agent and got them right. Once we trimmed those instructions, the questions usually failed until we added a Page defining "in litigation."

We also tested whether Genie One could account for the user's team when interpreting a question.

We created two identities, one for Finance and one for Underwriting. Each told Genie One its team once, and Genie One Memory retained that information. Both identities then asked the same 12 questions in new conversations: seven where the correct answer depended on the team and five that asked for straightforward facts.

Finance identity Underwriting identity
"Did our loss ratio get better or worse from 2024 to 2025?" 8.2 points worse (calendar year, after reinsurance) 1.5 points better (policies written that year, before reinsurance, without catastrophes)
Questions that depend on the team 6 of 7 right on every repeat 7 of 7 right on every repeat
Plain facts (policies written, claims, premium written…) 5 of 5, same answers 5 of 5, same answers

Every answer explained which team's definition it was using. This shows learned and modeled knowledge working together, because Genie One combined what it remembered about each user with the definition that team had modeled. Both identities had exactly the same data access, so the difference came from the team context Genie One remembered, not from differences in what the identities could see. This was a test of business context, not access control. Remembering someone's team doesn't replace permissions or row-level security; those still need to be enforced separately.

Business definitions don't stay fixed. We wanted to see how much work it would take to update one without breaking the others.

Partway through, Underwriting decided its loss ratio should also include the legal cost of defending claims. We updated the Underwriting Metric View and added one sentence to its Page. We didn't change any agent instructions. Then we asked 12 questions about the Underwriting loss ratio through Genie One, with the curated agents and the governed layer in place.

Every answer used the new definition. Eight questions about definitions we didn't change stayed right. In the curated-only setup, the same change would have meant finding and editing the formula in seven places across four agents' instructions.

One caveat: the agents still held the old formula. Asked directly outside Genie One, they used it in 92% of answers with no warning and would keep doing so until someone updates each agent. Centralizing definitions reduces duplication, but any logic left in agents still needs maintenance.

We repeated the main comparison with a fictional retailer. Finance, Merchandising, and Marketing each had a different definition of revenue. We asked, "Did revenue grow in 2025?"

  • Merchandising, which counts everything ordered before discounts, reports growth of 13.6%.
  • Finance, which counts revenue when orders ship, after discounts and refunds, says it fell 9.4%.
  • Marketing, which counts completed orders before returns, says it stayed flat.

A holiday sale and a jump in clothing returns explain the gap, and all three are right.

The benchmark contained 49 questions, making this a smaller check of the pattern rather than a second full study.

Retail, through Genie One Curated agents Curated agents + governed layer
All questions 54% (41–67%) 82% (71–92%)
Definition questions 31% 100%
Answers using tables from outside this business 21% 6%
Answers using look-alike tables 5% 0%

The curated retail agents worked well on their own. Through Genie One, though, they got about half the questions right, because nothing in Unity Catalog said what revenue meant for each team or which tables belonged to the business. With the governed layer, definition accuracy jumped from 31% to 100%, and overall accuracy rose to 82%.

Based on these experiments, keep your curated agents and add a governed layer underneath them. The key decision is where each piece of information belongs:

Where What it holds
Certified Metric Views Scoped datasets with join keys, calculations, and dimensions that Genie One and Agents use to calculate and aggregate data
Domains and Subdomains Business and team ownership, with shared facts in the main Domain and team-specific context in Subdomains
Pages Explanations of business terms, pointing to the tables, views, and documents that hold the evidence. Pages can link to related assets relevant to the page, such as a Metric View.
Table and Metric View descriptions What the data covers and doesn't, including date ranges, missing budget or expense data
Agent instructions Behavior rules state which definition was used, ask for clarification when needed, and acknowledge when the data can't answer a question

A few practical lessons stood out:

  1. Start with definitions that mean different things to different teams, especially those that exist as tribal knowledge within a single team. Genie One already handles universally agreed-upon facts well.
  2. Define each measure once. Put the official calculation in a certified Metric View rather than maintaining the same formula in several agent instructions. In our tests, Metric Views and Pages drove the gains in accuracy. In our step-by-step test, certification steered Genie One away from look-alike decoy tables, cutting their use from 9% to 4%, and Domains and Pages took it to zero.
  3. Use Pages to explain the business context. Link them to the certified tables and Metric Views they describe. On each Page, define the scenarios where a calculation applies and the ones where Genie One should avoid it. A definition is more useful when Genie One can connect it to the underlying data.
  4. Keep agents focused on what they do best. Team-specific documents, Domain knowledge, and behavior rules still matter. The governed layer doesn't replace that context, particularly when a question depends on information that isn't represented in tables or Metric Views.
  5. Test through Genie One, not just through individual agents. An agent that answers well on its own won't help if Genie One doesn't route to it, so measure the end-to-end experience before and after each change.

To apply this to your own data, start with the terms your teams define differently, add them to a Domain/Subdomain with Metric Views and Pages, and measure the change through Genie One. The Genie Ontology documentation explains how the pieces fit together, and our guide to operationalizing Genie Ontology in your data stack walks through setting them up step by step.

entries.title: Four AI Architecture Patterns for Regulated Industries
entries.summary: Enterprise AI cannot replace every deterministic control. These four patterns help...
entries.content:
How to place determinism, agentic reasoning, human authority and bounded autonomy in enterprise systems

  • Four production architecture patterns for combining agents with deterministic controls and human accountability.
  • A decision framework for determining where agents may reason, generate, recommend, or act.
  • Why governed data, lineage, enforcement, evaluation, and audit evidence-not the model alone-make enterprise agents deployable.

Enterprise AI cannot replace every deterministic control. These four patterns help architects decide where agents can reason, act, and remain subject to controls or human authority.

Enterprises are adding agents to systems built on fixed rules and repeatable processes. Agents can reason through complex problems, but enterprise systems-especially in regulated industries-must remain controlled and auditable. The question is not which one to choose. It is how to make them work together.

We are writing this series because customers ask us the same questions: How are enterprises around the world navigating constraints similar to ours? What is the reality of enterprise AI adoption? How are other organizations approaching these nuances? How is Databricks helping solve them when the requirements are ambiguous, complex, and so specific to the institution?

We as Forward Deployed Engineers work at this boundary. We take ambiguous business problems and turn them into production-ready systems. While implementations will vary by institution and we cannot disclose specific implementation details, we can discuss generalized patterns and practices. As agents become part of large enterprise systems, two questions keep recurring:

  • Where must determinism remain (e.g., when actions are irreversible or errors carry asymmetric risk)?
  • Where can an agent be given authority, particularly if actions are reversible or low-cost to remediate?

The answer is not the same for every use case. Across the systems we are building and modernizing in the field, four patterns are emerging. This first article introduces the framework. The next four articles show how each pattern works in practice.

Use this pattern when outcomes must be strictly deterministic and reproducible, or when errors are irreversible and carry high remediation costs. Here, deterministic means the result can be reproduced under an explicit, versioned contract that records the data, rule, tolerance, configuration, and execution context together.

Financial Institutions have lots of controls. Reconciliations are a good example. The control must calculate the balances, apply an approved rule, and produce a reproducible PASS or FAIL. An agent cannot reinterpret the tolerance or turn its own explanation into a passed control. When a reconciliation fails, an agent can gather evidence, inspect lineage and batch status, compare the break with prior incidents, test a bounded set of causes, and recommend what should happen next. The deterministic control still decides whether the reconciliation passed. The agent helps explain why it failed.

The agent can investigate the control. It cannot become the control.

This pattern also applies to regulatory calculations, policy enforcement, data quality gates, and system integrity checks-anywhere the result must be precise, reproducible, and auditable.

Use this pattern when more than one answer may be valid, but the result can be tested objectively.

Legacy migration or modernization is a good example. An agent can analyze an existing workload and generate a target implementation. It may not produce exactly the same implementation each time. That is not necessarily a problem. What matters is whether the result is correct.

A deterministic judge can test whether the code compiles, schemas conform, data reconciles, control totals match, governance requirements are satisfied, and performance meets the target. If the result fails, the agent receives the evidence, diagnoses the problem, corrects its work, and runs through validation again.

Passing that judge proves that the candidate satisfied the approved acceptance contract. It does not prove that the contract covers every production behavior. Test coverage, production-shaped edge cases, and periodic review still matter.

Do not make the agent deterministic when you can deterministically evaluate its output.

The validator is not only a control. It is the feedback loop that allows the agent to improve its result. This pattern works well for migration, code generation, transformation, testing, and remediation.

Use this pattern when the answer requires judgment and cannot be proven correct by a deterministic test.

Financial crime investigations are one example. An agent can correlate transactions, documents, policies, relationships, and historical patterns. It can assemble evidence, identify likely explanations, surface unresolved questions, and recommend a disposition. This is also often required by regulation where a decision significantly affects a person, or when you have to justify the outcome to a regulator, auditor, court, or the affected person

But a recommendation is not a decision. When the outcome is consequential, and there is no deterministic way to establish correctness, authority must remain with an accountable person.

Human review should sit at the decision boundary, not inside every step.

The agent's reasoning must also often be explainable. Every recommendation should trace back to the evidence, sources, and tools behind it. That lets the investigator challenge the logic and lets auditors or regulators reconstruct how the agent reached its recommendation. Where regulation gives an affected person the right to an explanation, the explanation must be specific to the decision. It covers the main factors, the agent's role, and the human's role. "The model flagged it" is not enough. The investigator records the rationale for the final call, including any agent override.

The agent reduces investigative effort and improves the consistency of the evidence presented. The investigator retains responsibility for the final decision, which may be subjective and nuanced and not deterministic.

Use this pattern when the agent needs to act, but only within an explicit operating envelope.

Consider a Governance Intelligence module that manages access to governed enterprise data. A user describes what data they need, why they need it, and for how long. The agent interprets the request, identifies the appropriate data product, determines the minimum access required, and gathers the relevant identity, policy, ownership, classification, lineage, and usage context.

Requiring manual approval for every standard request creates delay without necessarily reducing risk. Giving the agent unrestricted authority to grant access creates an unacceptable control gap. The answer is bounded autonomy.

The operating envelope defines:

  • which data products and access levels qualify for straight-through processing;
  • which identity, purpose, geography, legal entity, residency, and segregation of duties rules must pass;
  • the maximum duration and minimum level of access that may be granted;
  • which approved Unity Catalog actions the agent may initiate;
  • which sensitive, ambiguous, or exceptional requests require human approval; and
  • how access is monitored, expired, revoked, and recorded for audit.

Within that envelope, the agent can interpret the request, assemble the evidence, select the approved workflow, and initiate a time-bound entitlement. Deterministic policy services validate every required condition before Unity Catalog enforces the grant.

Do not try to constrain every decision. Constrain the operating envelope. Implementing multi-agent judge frameworks across validation cycles within this envelope can also complement human oversight with automated, multi-perspective safety checks.

If the request falls outside the envelope - for example, because it involves sensitive data, missing attributes, conflicting policies, excessive privilege, or a segregation of duties exception- the system blocks straight through execution and routes it to the appropriate data owner, steward, or risk reviewer.

Databricks provides the governed foundation across the four patterns. Omnigent can compose agents and agent harnesses without making any one agent the architecture. Unity Gateway governs access to models, tools, MCP servers, and external APIs. Unity Catalog governs enterprise data and enforces approved access including residency and cross-border transfer rules. Secure connectivity reaches on-premises, cloud, and SaaS systems without bypassing these control points. MLflow preserves traces and evaluation evidence that also serve as audit records for regulators. See the attached diagram for a reference architecture showing how agent calls flow through governed control points to customer systems across on-premises, cloud, and regulated jurisdictions.

Traditional modernization changes where and how technology runs. AI transformation changes the execution model itself. Systems that primarily followed predefined instructions can now interpret, reason, generate, and act.

That does not mean discarding the deterministic systems enterprises have spent decades building. In many cases, those systems become the foundation of the agentic architecture:

  • Policy engines become control planes.
  • Validation frameworks become deterministic judges.
  • Acceptance criteria become agent evaluations.
  • Operational limits become autonomy boundaries.
  • Governed data, lineage, and audit trails provide the context and evidence agents need.

The opportunity is not simply to replace legacy systems with agents. Across all four patterns, what makes an agent deployable is the ground it stands on: governed enterprise data, verifiable lineage, enforced access, measurable quality, and a reproducible audit trail.

This is especially important in regulated industries, where a weak architectural boundary can lead to control failures, penalties, or delayed regulatory commitments. A well-designed boundary can reduce investigative effort, shorten modernization cycles, and enable high-value automation without transferring inappropriate authority to the model.

AI-native architecture is about deciding where determinism, intelligence, and authority should live.

Before designing an agentic solution, ask three questions:

  • What may the agent reason about?
  • What may the agent be allowed to do?
  • What must remain outside the agent’s authority?

Those answers determine whether the solution needs a deterministic control, a deterministic judge, a human decision boundary, or an explicit operating envelope. The model comes after that architectural decision-not before it.

The patterns are not mutually exclusive. A production system may use a deterministic control for one decision, human authority for an exception, and bounded autonomy for an approved remediation. The important point is to make each boundary explicit.

As systems mature in production, these boundaries can adapt: deterministic judges refine their evaluation rules using accumulated usage data, while human authority boundaries can shift as feedback establishes confidence in agent reasoning.

The next four articles take each pattern from architecture to implementation:

Part 2: Deterministic control and agentic reasoning

How agents can investigate exceptions around deterministic financial controls without weakening enforcement or auditability.

Part 3: Agentic execution and a deterministic judge

How agents can generate and correct implementations while deterministic validation decides whether the result is acceptable.

Part 4: Agentic reasoning and human authority

How Lakewatch can combine monitoring signals, bank data, and specialist network intelligence into a reviewable evidence package while an accountable investigator retains the consequential decision.

Part 5: Agentic execution with bounded autonomy

A design blueprint for agents to coordinate governed data access inside a policy-defined operating envelope, with deterministic authorization, Unity Catalog enforcement, and human resolution of material exceptions.

Classify your use case using the four-pattern framework, then continue to the implementation article that matches the boundary your system requires. For regulated use cases that cross multiple patterns, contact your Databricks account team or FDE engagement manager to map the control, reasoning, and authority boundaries before selecting the agent architecture.

Molly Nagamuthu is a Principal Forward Deployed Engineer at Databricks. She works with enterprises on complex data and AI transformation initiatives, particularly with global banks where modernization must coexist with governance, controls, and operational rigor.

In this series, Molly and other Forward Deployed Engineers share implementation patterns emerging from work in the field as enterprises move from deterministic architectures toward AI-native systems.

Every Azure Databricks user gets a free monthly Genie allowance, and admins decide whether anyone spends beyond it, so partners can recommend Genie with predictable costs.

by David Meyer and Robert Saxby

  • Every Azure Databricks user gets $10 of free Genie usage a month, and Genie budgets let admins control any spend beyond it.
  • The Genie ontology reduces AI spend by “saving the work” the whole company has already done in a governed memory.
  • With smart routing and open-weight models, Genie keeps getting cheaper, and the more customers use it, the more efficient it becomes.

Every Azure Databricks user gets $10 of free Genie usage each month, usage that many AI tools charge for. And Genie is built to get cheaper as customers use it. The Genie ontology saves the work the whole company has already done, so Genie doesn't redo it for every question. Smart routing and open-weight models keep lowering the cost of each answer, and the more customers use Genie, the more efficient it becomes. Genie budgets let admins decide whether anyone spends beyond the free allowance. For partners, that turns the cost question into a reason to roll Genie out broadly.

If you advise customers on AI, you’ve likely seen this: once they experience what Genie can do, they want it everywhere, in front of every employee and not just a pilot team. What they need next is a path to scale it within cost boundaries. Some customers block consumption-based AI tools entirely, and others hold off on a trial because they worry about what happens to costs as usage grows.

That concern is reasonable. As AI moves from a few pilot users to the whole workforce, finance teams want predictable costs and clear guardrails before they say yes. Genie is built to meet that bar: every user gets free monthly usage so everyone can benefit, and budget controls are ready for when usage ramps.

For partners, that means you can help customers adopt AI across their enterprise without cost limiting the conversation. You can start broad with cost controls in place from day one, which builds trust and makes it easier to scale. Genie’s pricing also complements the Microsoft 365 investments customers have already made.

Which Genie experience fits each customer?

  • Genie One: The AI coworker that gives every business user instant access to governed data and AI, with business context built in. For partners, it's the broadest entry point: roll it out to an entire customer org and let users ask questions in natural language, with no setup per user.
  • Genie Agents: No-code agents where data teams set up trusted data, metrics and business rules that power Genie One answers. For partners, this is where delivery work lives: configuring the right tables, metrics and instructions so the customer's business users get accurate, governed answers.
  • Genie Code: The autonomous AI agent that helps data teams plan, build and run data engineering, machine learning and AI workflows on Azure Databricks. For partners, it accelerates delivery: developers and data engineers use it to write, debug and ship pipelines faster.

All three are governed through Unity Catalog, so partners can match the right experience to each customer conversation and know the same access rules apply throughout.

Every identified user gets $10 of free Genie usage each month, and it resets on the first of every month. Even better, through January 31, 2027, Genie One and Genie Agents are free for users, so the full $10 goes to Genie Code. After that, the $10 allowance is shared across Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code.

Budgets apply only to pay-as-you-go usage above the free allowance. They can't remove it, so every user keeps the same free starting point.

Genie's cost story improves as customers use it:

  • The ontology saves the work. Genie keeps the context the whole company has built, such as trusted data, metrics and business rules, in a governed memory, so answers don't have to be recomputed from raw data or documents every time.
  • Smart routing and open-weight models. Genie sends each request to a cost-efficient model that can handle it, and open-weight models keep lowering the cost of each answer.
  • More use, more efficiency. The more people use Genie, the more saved context it can reuse, so each answer gets more efficient.

Genie budgets live in the account console and give admins tools to monitor spending, set limits and manage billable Genie usage:

  • Stay on the free allowance. Set a $0 per-user threshold with Block usage enabled. Users get their full free allowance, and Genie Code usage pauses once it runs out and resumes on the first of the month. Genie One and Genie Agents usage by users stays free through January 31, 2027.
  • Add headroom per user. A $30 per-user threshold sets a monthly spending limit of $30 per user, on top of the free allowance.
  • Set limits by group. Combine a shared threshold, a default per-user limit and higher overrides for specific users or groups.
  • Alert before blocking. Use alert-only thresholds to watch usage trends before setting limits.

A few details are worth telling customers up front. Budgets track each user’s spend in near real time and block new requests once a threshold is reached. Because tracking is an estimate, actual spend can land slightly above or below the threshold, and requests already in progress finish. Budgets are built for near-real-time spend control rather than as an absolute cap, and warehouse compute is billed separately. Service principals don’t get the free allowance, so automated usage is billed.

Start with spend control, not a procurement cycle

Most enterprise AI projects begin with a business case and a procurement cycle. With Genie, customers can start with spend control instead: set the pay-as-you-go threshold to $0, roll Genie out broadly on the free allowance, learn how people actually use it and add budget only where the value is clear.

Genie brings governed Azure Databricks data into Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Cowork, Excel and Copilot Studio, with Unity Catalog permissions applied throughout. Users ask questions where they already work, and the answers respect the same access rules as the rest of their data. The Azure Databricks Genie Plugin, now generally available, gives partners a one-step way to bring Genie into a customer's Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot environment, so the first conversation can happen in minutes.

For example, business users can ask questions about their company's data directly from Teams or Copilot, bring Genie results into Excel, or use Genie to power agents built in Copilot Studio. Some integrations are in preview and may require additional setup or licensing.

For partners, this opens opportunities to connect AI to existing business workflows, build new solutions and help customers get more value from their Microsoft and Databricks investments. Plugging Genie into Microsoft 365 Copilot doesn't mean paying twice: Copilot routes the questions Genie can answer to Genie, so customers avoid those costs on the Copilot side.

  • A free starting point for every customer. Every user gets $10 of free Genie usage a month, and Genie One and Genie Agents are free for users through January 31, 2027, so partners can open the AI conversation without a cost hurdle.
  • An answer to the finance question. Starting at a $0 pay-as-you-go threshold lets partners address cost concerns before they come up.
  • Confidence to scale. Alert-only thresholds let real usage set the limits, so budgets are based on data rather than guesses.
  • A way into Microsoft 365 conversations. Genie connects governed data to the tools customers already use.
  • The right Genie for every audience. Genie One for business users, Genie Agents for the data teams who set up trusted data, and Genie Code for data engineers and developers.
  • A cost story that improves over time. The ontology, smart routing and open-weight models make Genie more efficient as customers use it, so the cost case gets stronger as adoption grows.

For SIs: Genie is a low-friction way into every Microsoft 365 account. Open with a broad rollout at $0 in pay-as-you-go spend, then build services around it: budget and persona design, Unity Catalog governance, Genie setup and expansion into new use cases.

For ISVs: If your product works with Unity Catalog data, Genie can bring that governed data into Teams and Copilot for your joint customers.

Learn: Manage budgets and cost controls for Genie, the Genie consumption guide and the Genie cost and budgets FAQ

For partners: Get enabled on Genie and Azure Databricks through partner training on the Databricks Partner Academy, and talk to your Databricks partner team or Partner Solutions Architect about demos and co-sell.

Every identified user also gets $10 of free Genie Code usage each month. After that date, the $10 monthly allowance is shared across Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code. Each user has their own allowance, and it resets on the first of every month. Usage above it is billed pay-as-you-go, and admins can control that spend with Genie budgets. The allowance covers Genie's AI usage only. SQL warehouse compute is billed separately, and service principals don't get a free allowance.

Genie budgets let admins set spending thresholds in the account console for pay-as-you-go Genie usage above the free allowance. Admins can set shared, per-user and group thresholds, use alert-only thresholds or block usage once a threshold is reached. Budgets can't remove a user's free allowance.

Yes. Set a $0 per-user threshold with Block usage enabled. Users get their full free allowance, and Genie Code usage pauses once it runs out and resumes on the first of the month.

Yes. Genie brings governed Azure Databricks data into Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Excel and Copilot Studio, with Unity Catalog permissions applied throughout. The Azure Databricks Genie Plugin gives partners a one-step way to add Genie to a customer's Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot environment. Some integrations are in preview and may require additional setup or licensing.

Further, Copilot knows what Genie can answer and routes appropriate questions to Genie, avoiding those costs on the Copilot side. entries.content:
As of November 19 at 10 AM Pacific Time:

Prior to Java4Shell’s public disclosure (CVE-2026-114938), Databricks was already addressing the industry-wide OpenJDK vulnerability.

Databricks is protecting customers in two phases: quick mitigation to disable use of the vulnerable code, and then patching to replace the vulnerable code.

  • Mitigation: We have applied the mitigation to our platform, disabling use of vulnerable code for all supported versions of Databricks Runtime. We do not expect the mitigation to have a meaningful performance impact on customers. In order to apply the mitigation as quickly as possible, we have taken the rare step of proactively restarting affected clusters.
  • Patching: While the mitigation blocks the attack, in an abundance of caution, we will be providing patched versions of supported Databricks Runtimes. Customers on our serverless platform will automatically get them. Customers with classic clusters will need to restart their clusters.

We are also reaching out to customers running custom images.

We have no evidence to indicate any unauthorized access to Databricks products, services, or customers' data.
